leads.work: Darron Giron re-forwards the daily Credit Report (the list of TAGG deals to rebook or pending with credit) by hand to one of his staff (Carole Frank, Ryan O'Rourke or Patrick Ryder), almost every business day. While he was on vacation the reports backed up and he forwarded them in a batch afterwards.
leads.why: Credit (Veronica Espinoza, Russell Diamond, Jason Williams, Darren Vanek) sends the report to a list of about 35 people. Each desk lead then forwards it to whoever handles it on his desk. This batch has about 50 of these forwards and they add nothing. The distribution list could include those staff directly, or the rebook actions could go to them automatically.

leads.work: Deals in TAGG are rebooked by hand to the correct legal entity or counterparty, as credit directs: parent and affiliate name fixes, ENA to ECC under the ISDA, and RiskMantra to ENA.
leads.why: Each day's credit report lists many rebooks with the same pattern, for example 'Rebook to Aquila Risk Management', 'Rebook to BP Amoco Corporation' and 'Rebook ENA trades to ECC'. Credit staff also send one-off rebook requests, and Giron forwards them on. The same counterparties come up again and again, which suggests the counterparty or entity at deal capture (EOL or TAGG) could be checked against rules or mapped automatically.

leads.work: Canadian deals, especially Aquila Canada Corp. and Engage Energy Canada, have to be found and 'flipped' by hand from Houston books to the FT-US/CAND-ERMS (P&) book. If this is missed, liquidations have to be re-run and invoices are missed.
leads.why: Stacey Vallejo sent these requests again and again over a month to all the desk leads. She writes that 'the EOL group is still working on a solution'. She asks the leads to search all their books for these deals, and one deal that was not flipped forced the February liquidations to be re-run. A booking rule tied to the counterparty would remove this work.

leads.work: Meters have recorded gas flow but no nomination, or the deal ticket has expired. Logistics and settlements staff email the trader (Daren Farmer) one meter at a time to extend the deal, create a new ticket or set a volume, so that allocation can run or a sale can be drafted in Unify.
leads.why: This batch has a dozen or more of these requests, phrased the same way each time, for example 'meter has flow and no nom' or 'deal expired, should it be extended?'. They create allocation exceptions and hold up invoicing. A rule to roll evergreen or gathering-point deals forward, or an exception report, could replace the emails.

leads.work: When a counterparty's invoice or payment shows a price that differs from the Sitara deal price, settlements emails the trader or risk to confirm the price and change the deal, one deal at a time.
leads.why: The pattern repeats across TXU, Conoco, BP, Crosstex, Southern Union, Guadalupe and CP&L. In one case, monthly price updates on deal 27253 are requested every month. The requests go back and forth among several people, and one invoice was delayed because the trader was out. Index-based or WACOG pricing could be set up in the system, or the reconciliation could be automated.

leads.work: Each month, curve validation questions arrive from Jennifer Nguyen. Desk leads have to explain why forward curves moved (SOCAL, PGE Topock, CIG WIC and others), often by asking the traders.
leads.why: This is a monthly cycle seen for January, February and March. The answers repeat ('market traded higher'), and there is back-and-forth when the answers are judged too thin. The same curve, Topock, is said to 'show up every month'. The commentary could be templated, or the validation thresholds reconsidered.

leads.work: Jim Little asks the desk leads by hand for liquidation flash support by region and month. The supporting files are saved to the ERMS/FRED Liquidations folder.
leads.why: These requests recur for each month (November, December, January) and include volume files. He has to remind leads to save support for all months. This could be a standard report saved on a schedule.

leads.work: Requests from Arthur Andersen auditors for deal tickets, confirmations and forwards detail ('monthly gas testing', quarterly checklist) are forwarded down the chain and followed up late.
leads.why: The testing is described as 'monthly'. The quarterly checklist goes only to desk leads, who have to forward it on, and one request was missed for two weeks during a vacation. A shared request tracker or a standard extract could help.

leads.work: OA (operational accounting) and flash-to-actual variances are investigated by hand, for example a PGEV park-and-lend imbalance that was never flashed in CPR, and a Gas Accounting project to collect the physical storage inventory schedules.
leads.why: Rita Wynne says the imbalance is booked 'every month' and causes an OA variance. Giron admits that he takes small variances 'without looking into the underlying cause'. Gossett collected suggested improvements for OA, and Jim Pond chased storage information to reduce flash-to-actual variances. The variances recur and are worked by hand.

leads.work: For the GLO/EGM gas/crude swap, a set of manual deal ticket steps has to be done every month before flash: zero out the price, enter demand charges between HPL and ENA, and enter the ENA sale to EGM.
leads.why: Bryce Baxter lays out four tickets that 'will require the following steps be taken monthly'. Settlement later asks for clarification of these entries. This is a fixed monthly calculation that could be automated.

leads.work: Pipeline imbalance and volume reconciliation are done by hand: Big Cowboy/GEPL overproduction, under-nomination at King Ranch, the Oasis transport imbalance, and an ad hoc list of gas owed compiled from the RTU variance and imbalance reports.
leads.why: Mary Poorman writes that the issue is 'ongoing every month' at 6–10 thousand per day for six months. She asks for meter statements to be faxed and builds spreadsheets by hand. She compiled the list of points owed gas 'urgently' from several reports.

leads.work: Weekend and after-hours on-call notes are written up and emailed to the whole logistics team. The on-call schedule and the weekend systems availability notice are also distributed by email.
leads.why: These are recurring weekly emails. The notes record confirm changes and calls with gas control that might be better kept in a shared log.

leads.work: Cheryl Dudley prepares the monthly HPL Assignment, Termination and Expiration report by hand and maintains its distribution list by hand. There is also confusion over contract termination and evergreen terms, and over drafting shut-in letters.
leads.why: The report is done monthly and was once skipped by accident. The termination letter request produced a three-way exchange because the contract system recorded no evergreen while the confirmation had evergreen language, so the contract data was not reliable.

leads.work: Coordination of the HPL sale to AEP: a transition-issues memo revised repeatedly, deal download files, transport contract assignment, and procedures being drafted for requests (counterparties, books, security, curve mapping).
leads.why: Bob Hall sends repeated drafts and asks everyone for changes. The procedures named would become an ongoing formal protocol of manual requests for AEP. This is a time cost now and may create recurring work later.

leads.work: Ad hoc data requests to desk leads are collected by email: penalty charges by counterparty, MTM values by region for given dates, trader website access lists, analyst/associate needs, and brown bag training topics.
leads.why: Each request goes to all desk leads, who forward it to their staff and consolidate the replies, often with reminders sent. The penalty data was pulled from many settlement analysts 'before you leave today'.

leads.work: System access, user list and book setup are administered by email: RiskTrac upload users, Logic On/Off script users, Book Admin web access, trading group assignments for books, renaming the Denver books, new-hire applications and passwords, and listing ODBC DSNs and machines.
leads.why: There are several separate requests to different admins. Giron says it would help if new people had 'all of their applications and passwords ready to go' when they start. Renaming the Denver books would require changing 'every deal' by hand.

leads.work: Origination grants and credit reserves are handled by email between originators, credit and risk, and errors have to be corrected.
leads.why: A $100K amount was granted twice by mistake and had to be reversed. Originators chase whoever is responsible for granting origination. Each reserve is taken by email memo.

leads.work: Giron approves the preliminary Enovate DPR (daily position report) each day by email reply.
leads.why: There are 'For your approval' emails for consecutive days with replies of 'OK'. This is a routine daily sign-off that could be built into a workflow.

leads.work: Logistics schedulers ask traders by email for deal numbers or ticket changes to confirm nominations: Equistar noms, Duke meter breakdowns, Kinder Morgan net-out notes for settlements, Exxon bid spreadsheets, and the Oasis online nomination signup.
leads.why: These exchanges recur at the start of each month (first-of-month noms). Faxes and email are used where online nomination systems exist.

leads.work: HR and training administration is done by email: performance review reviewer nominations, PBA nominations, and course registration approvals that return errors.
leads.why: These are recurring review-cycle tasks. The course approval link failed. Each is a small amount of time that comes back every period.

leads.work: A large share of the employee mailbox is non-business email: chain jokes, personal forwards and lunch planning.
leads.why: Dozens of personal forwards were sent to many internal and external recipients. This is a minor time and mail-load cost and a possible policy issue.
